opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a lot of ways in, and it doesn't all have to be from inside a lab.

If you're inside a lab, a big one is just engaging with the policy as a real thing that affects your work. A responsible scaling policy is only as good as its implementation. Someone on a training team, like my team, notices practical issues: an evaluation can't run at the point in training where it needs to, or a commitment is ambiguous once you're actually running a big model. Raising those things, and pushing for the policy to be precise enough that you'd know if you were violating it, is really valuable. It also helps to have a culture where people feel comfortable saying "I think we're close to a threshold" without that being seen as slowing things down.

For people working on evaluations specifically, there's a lot of hard, unglamorous work to do. Good evals for dangerous capabilities, like serious uplift for bioweapons, autonomous replication, or cyber offense, are hard to build. You want them to be predictive, hard to game, and not saturated the moment a new model comes out. You also want to be able to elicit the model's full capabilities, because if your eval underestimates what the model can do, the whole framework rests on a false sense of security. There's a lot of room for researchers to make these more rigorous.

Outside the labs, I think external researchers and third-party evaluators matter a lot. Labs grading their own homework only goes so far, so organizations that can independently test models, or critique the methodology, add real accountability. Policy people can help turn voluntary commitments into norms or regulation, so labs that take this seriously aren't disadvantaged against labs that don't. And honestly, people who just read these policies closely and write public critiques, saying "this threshold is vague" or "this commitment doesn't actually bind you to anything," are doing something useful. We've updated our thinking based on that kind of feedback.

The broader point is that these frameworks are early. Nobody has this figured out, so there's a lot of value in people from different backgrounds poking at them and helping make them more concrete and more credible over time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building rigorous evaluations and independent testing, but does not say that providing ready-to-run evaluations makes adoption easier for busy AI companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the things I'm most excited about, because the responsible scaling policy is explicitly designed to be a living document. We've said from the start that we expect it to be wrong in places and that we'll revise it as we learn more. So there's a lot of room for people to contribute, and the ways to do that look pretty different depending on where you sit.

If you're inside a lab, the most direct thing is working on the evaluations themselves. The whole framework rests on being able to say "the model can't yet do X" with some confidence, and right now that's a hard scientific problem. We don't have great tools for eliciting the full capabilities of a model, we don't know how much a determined actor with fine-tuning access could get out of it, and our evals for things like bioweapons uplift or autonomous replication are still pretty early. So if you're a researcher who can make those evals more rigorous, or figure out how to measure whether an eval is actually tracking the dangerous capability rather than some proxy, that's enormously valuable. Honestly, I think it's one of the highest-leverage things a technical person can work on right now, because the evals are the load-bearing part.

The other internal piece is just holding the policy to account. One of the things I like about having a written commitment is that it gives employees something concrete to point at. If you see a place where the company isn't living up to what it said, you can say "this doesn't match what we committed to," and that's a much stronger position than a vague sense that something feels off. I'd encourage people at labs to actually read these documents carefully and push on them, because a policy that nobody internally is scrutinizing isn't worth much.

If you're outside the labs, I think the critical role is honestly critique. We put the policy out publicly partly so that people could poke holes in it, and some of the most useful feedback has come from people who have no affiliation with us saying "this threshold is too vague" or "this doesn't address the following scenario." Researchers at academic groups, at organizations like METR or the AI Safety Institutes, can run independent evaluations, build better benchmarks, and in general make it harder for any lab to grade its own homework. I think the ecosystem is a lot healthier when there's third-party capacity to actually verify the claims labs are making, rather than just taking our word for it.

And then there's the policy side. Right now these are voluntary commitments, and a voluntary commitment only binds the people who've made it. If you're working in government or on policy, there's a real question of how you take the useful parts of these frameworks, the idea that you define capability thresholds in advance and tie safeguards to them, and turn that into something with more teeth that applies across the industry. I don't think labs should be the ones designing that regulation, but I do think the people working on it benefit a lot from understanding how the internal frameworks actually work in practice, including where they're weak.

The last thing I'd say is that you don't have to be a safety specialist to help. A lot of what makes a scaling policy succeed or fail is pretty mundane: whether the security team actually has the resources to hit the security standards, whether the infrastructure exists to run evals quickly enough that they don't get skipped under deadline pressure, whether the people deciding when to pause have real authority. Engineers, security people, managers, even recruiters who are deciding who to hire all shape whether the policy is something that gets followed or something that sits on a website. So I'd encourage people to think about how their particular role connects to that, rather than assuming it's someone else's job.

r001.rationale: The response supports improving evaluations and building independent benchmarks, and mentions infrastructure for running evaluations quickly. It does not say that providing ready-to-run evaluations makes adoption easier for busy AI companies.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different ways to contribute, depending on your role. If you’re a researcher, one important contribution is making evaluations better at detecting the capabilities we’re actually worried about. What would count as evidence that a model could substantially help someone cause harm? And how do you test for that reliably, especially when a model might have a capability that your initial prompting doesn’t reveal?

If you work inside a lab, you can help turn those evaluations into decisions. A responsible scaling policy needs to specify what happens when a threshold is reached: what additional safeguards are required, who decides whether they’re sufficient, and what you do if you can’t establish that they are. There’s a lot of practical work in making those commitments clear enough that they guide behaviour under pressure.

People outside labs can contribute independent evaluations and scrutinise the policies. Are the thresholds meaningful? Could an evaluation miss something important? Do the commitments actually address the risks they’re supposed to address? Having people who can ask those questions with technical depth is valuable.

And policymakers can help establish expectations for evidence and accountability across labs. I’d want that work to stay closely connected to what we can actually measure, while recognising that an evaluation passing doesn’t establish that a system is safe.

Across those roles, the useful thing is to make the connection between evidence and action more concrete. What do we need to know, how will we find it out, and what will we do differently depending on the result?

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving evaluations and translating results into lab decisions, but it does not say to provide ready-to-run evaluations or that doing so makes adoption easier for busy AI companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different places where people can contribute. Inside a lab, there’s the technical work of making evaluations actually informative: figuring out which capabilities would be dangerous, designing tests for those capabilities, and checking that you’re eliciting what the model can really do. A model failing to do something in your evaluation isn’t necessarily strong evidence that it couldn’t do it with better prompting or different tools.

But there’s also a lot of work translating those results into decisions. What result would cause you to pause? What safeguards would you need before proceeding? Who has the authority to make that call? Researchers, security engineers, and people working on policy and governance all have a role there. You want those commitments to be clear before you’re facing a consequential decision under commercial pressure.

Outside the labs, independent researchers can develop better evaluations and point out gaps in existing policies. Governments and civil society can scrutinise whether the commitments are meaningful and whether there’s enough external accountability. And people who understand particular areas of risk can help identify things that a general-purpose evaluation team might miss.

The common thread is making these policies concrete enough that they change behaviour. It’s relatively easy to say that you’ll be careful as models become more capable. The useful work is establishing what you’ll measure, what you’ll do in response, and how anyone can tell whether you followed through.

r001.rationale: The response discusses developing better evaluations, but does not say that providing ready-to-run evaluations makes adoption easier for busy AI companies.
